name: Julio Le Parc
bio: Julio Le Parc (born 1928) grew up in Argentina, studied at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Buenos Aires and moved to Paris in 1958. In 1960 he co-founded the Groupe de Recherche d'Art Visuel (GRAV), which wanted to replace the passive contemplation of a single masterpiece with works that viewers activate with their bodies and eyes. His experiments ran in several directions at once: black-and-white and fourteen-colour paintings built from strict systems; 'continual light' boxes and mobiles of hanging reflective plates that scatter moving light across walls; mirrored blades, distorting surfaces and games that make the viewer unstable on their feet. He won the Grand Prize for Painting at the 1966 Venice Biennale and was briefly expelled from France for his part in the protests of May 1968. Recent installations are huge spheres of hanging coloured plates. Tate Modern's retrospective Julio Le Parc: Light. Colour. Action. runs from June 2026 to May 2027.
studyNotes: The viewer completes the work. Light, mirrors and movement only come alive when someone walks past, looks, plays or loses their balance.
Systems behind the colour. His paintings use a fixed set of fourteen colours arranged by rules; compare how the same rule produces many compositions.
Simple means, big effects. Hanging plates, a lamp and a motor produce rooms full of moving light; the mechanism is never hidden.
Art as a democratic act. GRAV rejected the cult of the artist and the precious object; look for how the works invite anyone to take part.
